newsitem.title: USA: Dlr/mark cools down, dlr/yen edges up at U.S. noon.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/mark cools down, dlr/yen edges up at U.S. noon.

text.p: The dollar reversed course during U.S. morning trade, paring gains made versus the mark in Europe and rising toward the top of its narrow trading range against the yen.

Comments by German Chancellor Helmut Kohl may have eased concerns that arose earlier in the session that proposed European Monetary Union would be delayed or weakened by loosely interpreted entry rules, dealers said.
"Kohl's comments leaned more toward a narrow EMU. I think that's going to have some impact," said Mark Gargano, head of currency derivatives at First Union Corp.
Kohl was quoted as saying Germany would not allow loose EMU entry rules interpretation and would stick to the deficit target at three percent of gross domestic product.
The dollar had risen to a 40-month high at 1.7465 marks overnight and again in early U.S. trade amid public political wrangling over EMU in Germany.
At midday, the dollar stood down slightly at 1.7433/38 marks from 1.7438/43 at the open, but up from its U.S. session low at 1.7390. Dollar/yen rose to 114.45/55 from 114.33/43.
Strong U.S. economic data boosted U.S. interest rates and may have helped dollar/yen in early trade, dealers said.
The 30-year U.S. Treasury bond fell nearly a point as the Chicagoland Business Barometer rose to 61.5 in June from 56.8 in May and May home sales saw their best gain in six months.
"Now we believe the U.S. is having inflation again, so people are going out and selling bonds," Gargano said.
Dollar/yen failed to escape a narrow range between 114.25 and 114.75, but dealers said the mild gains offset negative chart patterns and reassured dollar bulls.
"Dollar/yen has been nice and quiet, just the way the authorites want it, said John Hazelton at Manufacturers and Traders Bank.
Hazelton, M&T's chief trader, noted the dollar remains fully valued, particulary against the mark, but continues to enjoy solid bidding interest in the face of EMU confusion and weak European data.
"It's not exactly wildly bullish at these levels, but there's nothing on the horizon to change things," he added.

The Federal Open Market Committee meets Tuesday and Wednesday and while very few observers see an imminent increase in U.S. interest rates, the prospect of rate hikes is certainly stronger in the United States than Europe or Japan, dealers noted.
In fact, last week's rate hike in Canada and the strong British economy are helping boost those nations' currencies as well, dealers said.

"We've seen a sterling, dollar and Canadian dollar play. All three (countries) look to be in a tightening mode and will probably gain on everything else," said Mike Malpede, senior foreign exchange analyst at Refco Group Ltd.
Sterling/mark hit a five year high at 2.9070, helping support dollar/mark, dealers said.
In other trade, the dollar was flat at 1.4595/05 Swiss francs. Sterling fell to $1.6640/50 from $1.6648/58.
The dollar rose to Canadian $1.3804/09 from C$1.3782/87.
((--Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664))
